Introduction
How
Note: Lessons XI.A.-D. are often taught together & therefore have been combined into a single lesson here
RM: Instrument Flying Hazards 								AI.XI.A.R1
Failure to Maintain VFR
Risks include disorientation, loss of control, getting lost, icing, stress, midair/terrain collision, & more
Spatial Disorientation & Loss of Control
Lack of orientation about the position, attitude, or movement of the airplane in space
In visual flight, the eyes prevail over any false sensations
In IMC, the eyes cannot correct for false sensations which can lead to disorientation
For more details, see II.A. Human Factors
Stress & Fatigue
Inadvertent IMC is a stressful and mentally fatiguing exercise, especially to the non-proficient pilot
Pilot Actions (Mitigation)
Keep proficient in flight by reference to instruments
Statistics show that a pilot who isn’t trained in instrument flying, or has let their skills erode, loses control after about 10 minutes once forced to rely solely on instruments
“We don’t rise to the level of our expectations; we fall to the level of our training”
Thorough preflight planning & weather briefings (weather reports/charts, alternates, terrain avoidance)
Have a general plan (automation, ATC, GPS, etc.) to safely navigate to an airport
In the case unexpected weather results in less than VMC, use all options to safely exit:
Flight Instruments – Transition to & trust the instruments
Automation – Use it to make your job easier
ATC – Request assistance (Other options: Guard, FSS, other aircraft, cell phone, etc.)
GPS – The moving map & magenta line can be great for SA
RM: Assistance & Emergencies 								AI.XI.A.R2
An emergency can either be a distress or urgency condition
Distress: Threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and of requiring immediate assistance
Do not hesitate to declare an emergency (ex: fire, mechanical failure, structural damage)
Urgency: Concerned about safety, requiring timely but not immediate help; potential distress condition
An aircraft is at least in an urgency condition the moment the pilot becomes doubtful about position, fuel endurance, weather, or any other condition that could adversely affect flight safety
This is the time to ask for help, not after it develops into a distress situation
Control and Performance
Pitch + Power = Performance
3 Instrument Categories:
Control - Display immediate attitude and power indications and permit precise adjustments
Control is determined by reference to the attitude indicator & power indicators
Control covers the Pitch + Power portion of the equation
Performance - Indicate the aircraft’s actual performance
Altimeter, airspeed indicator, VSI, heading indicator, and turn coordinator
Navigation - Indicate the position in relation to a selected navigation facility or fix
Determined by course / range indicators, glide-slope indicators, and bearing pointers
Procedural Steps
Establish - an attitude and power setting on the control instruments to obtain desired performance
Trim - until control pressures are neutralized
Crosscheck - the performance instruments to determine if the desired performance is being obtained
Adjust - the attitude or power setting on the control instruments as necessary, trim and repeat
Establish 								AI.XI.A.K1a, AI.XI.A.K1b, AI.XI.A.K1c
Set known/approximate pitch and power settings for the desired performance
Control instruments are used to set the pitch & bank attitude and power setting
Attitude Indicator: Pitch & Bank Control
Operation
Horizon disk is attached to double gimbal
Remains in the same plane as the gyro and the plane pitches/rolls about it
Adjustable mini aircraft appears to be flying relative to the horizon
Limitations & Errors
Can spill if subjected to excessive pitch/bank attitudes (n/a to solid state/G1000 systems)
May be a slight nose-up indication during a rapid acceleration and vice versa
Possibility of a small bank angle and pitch error after a 180o turn
Tiny amounts of friction over time can cause precession/tilting
Erection mechanism (pull the knob) returns the gyro to the proper position
Throttle: Power Control
Pitch Control
Changes are made by changing the pitch attitude by precise amounts in relation to the horizon
Measured in degrees or bar widths
Bank Control
Changes are made by changing the bank attitude by precise amounts in relation to the bank scale
Power Control
Made by throttle adjustments and reference to the power indicators
Make changes with the throttle and then crosscheck the engine indicators
Don’t fixate on the engine indicators while setting the power
RM: Trim 												AI.XI.A.R8
Trim for hands off flight
Don’t fly with trim – Set pitch & power, then trim the control pressures away
Crosscheck 											AI.XI.A.K1d
The continuous and logical observation of instruments for attitude and performance information
Select Radial Crosscheck (most popular method)
“Hub and Spoke” Method (based off attitude indicator)
Attitude indicator is the hub/primary reference, performance instruments are the spokes
Move from the hub out to a spoke, back to the hub and repeat to another spoke, etc.
Crosscheck & Bank
Establish, then check the heading indicator and turn coordinator for desired performance
Crosscheck & Pitch
Establish, then check the altimeter, VSI, and airspeed indicator for desired performance
Crosscheck Errors
RM: Fixation 										AI.XI.A.R5
Staring at a single instrument
Occurs for a variety of reasons and eliminates the crosscheck of other pertinent instruments
RM: Omission 										AI.XI.A.R5
Omitting an instrument from the crosscheck
May be caused by failure to anticipate major instrument indications following attitude changes
Emphasis (VSI chasing is common as is emphasizing pitch or bank instruments)
Putting emphasis on a single instrument, instead of the necessary combination of instruments
We naturally tend to rely on the instrument most understood
RM: Instrument Interpretation 								AI.XI.A.R6
For the crosscheck to be effective, you must understand the information being received
Understand each instrument’s operation and the application of that knowledge to performance
Instrument Operation & Limitations 						AI.XI.A.K1a, AI.XI.A.K1c
Heading Indicator
Gyro turns in a vertical plane, sensing rotation about the plane’s vertical axis
Compass is used to set the appropriate heading, and rigidity causes it to maintain this heading
Precession causes heading to drift & Earth rotates 15o per hour
Precession + rotation means heading should be checked/reset every 15 min
Turn Coordinator
Canted gimbal allowing the gyro to sense both rate of roll as well as rate of turn
A rapid roll rate causes the mini aircraft to bank more steeply than a slow roll rate
Used to establish and maintain a standard-rate turn (3o per second)
Align the wing of the mini aircraft with the turn index
Airspeed Indicator
Differential pressure gauge indicating the difference between pitot and static pressure
Diaphragm receives pressure from pitot tube & instrument case receives pressure from static port
Increasing pitot pressure/decreasing static pressure expands the diaphragm and vice versa
Gearing indicates changes in airspeed
Altimeter
Measures absolute pressure of the ambient air, displays it as feet above selected pressure level
Air pressure tries to compress aneroid wafers while natural springiness tries to expand them
Compression and expansion move gears/linkages to change the altitude displayed
Adjustable barometric scale (Kollsman window)
Errors (Mechanical and Inherent)
Nonstandard Temperature
Warmer than standard air is less dense, pressure levels are farther apart
True altitude > Indicated altitude
Colder than standard air is denser, pressure levels are closer together
True altitude < Indicated altitude
Nonstandard Pressure
High pressure to Low pressure
As pressure decreases, the altimeter registers it as a climb
Pilot descends to maintain altitude
True altitude < Indicated altitude
The opposite applies from Low pressure to High pressure – True alt > Indicated alt
From hot to cold, or from high to low, look out below!
Vertical Speed Indicator
Differential pressure instrument
Diaphragm and casing are connected to static pressure
Diaphragm is directly connected while the case has a delayed connection
During a climb/descent, the diaphragm expands/contracts immediately, while pressure in the case remains the same for a short period
The difference in pressure is displayed as rate of climb
Adjust
Make the necessary adjustments on the attitude indicator, then repeat the process again
The amount of deviation from the desired performance will determine the magnitude of correction
Restrict the attitude indicator’s pitch displacement to 1 bar or ½ bar width up or down
Use a bank angle that approximates the degrees to turn, not to exceed 30o
Smooth, small adjustments lead to smooth, steady control
Straight-and-Level Flight 									AI.XI.A.K1b
Establish: Establish wings level/nose on the horizon on the attitude indicator; adjust power for cruise
Trim: Trim to relieve the control pressures
Crosscheck: Monitor the instruments for any performance deviations from straight-and-level flight
Adjust: Re-establish pitch and/or power to correct for deviations, trim, and repeat
Turns to Headings 										AI.XI.D.K1b
NOTE: Prior to entering the turn, determine turn direction and the angle of bank required
Establish: Use coordinated aileron and rudder to establish the desired bank on the attitude indicator
If a standard rate turn, use the turn coordinator
Adjust pitch to maintain altitude
Trim: Relieve the control pressures
Crosscheck: Monitor the instruments for any performance deviations from the turn
Adjust: Re-establish pitch and/or power to correct for deviations, trim, and repeat
Roll Out
Apply coordinated rudder and aileron pressure to level the wings on the attitude indicator
Depending on the rate of turn, rollout 5-10o before the desired heading
Or use ½ the bank angle or less as a reference for small turns
Adjust pitch and power for straight-and-level flight at cruise, crosscheck, adjust, and repeat
Constant Airspeed Climb 									AI.XI.B.K1b
Establish: Raise the nose to the approximate pitch attitude for the desired climb speed
Approaching climb speed, set power to the climb setting (full)
Trim: Relieve the control pressures
Crosscheck: Monitor the instruments for any performance deviations from the climb
Adjust: Re-establish pitch and/or power to correct for deviations, trim, and repeat
Adjust pitch to maintain the desired climb airspeed (1 bar or ½ bar width movements)
Level Off
Lead the altitude by 10% of the vertical speed (Ex: 500 fpm climb is led by 50’)
Establish - Reduce power, apply elevator pressure toward level flight on the attitude indicator
Trim – Relieve control pressures
Crosscheck - VSI, altimeter and attitude indicator should show level flight – repeat the process
Turning Climbs
Apply the climb procedures above, and establish the desired bank angle on the attitude indicator
Monitor turn performance on the heading indicator and turn coordinator
Small adjustments to pitch and power may be necessary to maintain airspeed in the turn
The instrument crosscheck will have to be accelerated as there is more information to take in
Constant Airspeed Descent 									AI.XI.C.K1b
Establish: Reduce power for the descent and maintain straight-and-level flight as airspeed decreases
Approaching descent speed, lower the nose with the attitude indicator to maintain descent speed
Trim: Relieve the control pressures
Crosscheck: Monitor the instruments for any performance deviations from the desired descent
Adjust: Re-establish pitch and/or power to correct for deviations, trim, and repeat
Adjust the pitch attitude to maintain the desired climb airspeed
Level Off
Lead the altitude by 10% of the vertical speed (EX: 500 fpm descent is led by 50’)
Establish - Introduce power and apply smooth steady elevator pressure toward a level attitude
Trim – Relieve control pressures
Crosscheck - VSI, altimeter and attitude indicator should show level flight – repeat the process
Turning Descents
Apply the same procedures as above, and establish the desired bank angle on the attitude indicator
Monitor turn performance on the heading indicator and turn coordinator
Small adjustments to pitch and power may be necessary to maintain airspeed in the turn
The instrument crosscheck will have to be accelerated as there is more information to take in
Common Errors 										AI.XI.A.K2
“Fixation,” “Omission,” and “Emphasis” errors during instrument cross-check
Improper instrument interpretation
Improper control applications
Failure to establish proper pitch, bank, or power adjustments during altitude, heading, speed corrections
Improper entry or level-off procedure (specific to Constant Airspeed Climbs and Descents)
Improper entry or roll-out procedure (specific to Turns to Headings)
Faulty trim procedure
RM: Hazards
Collision Hazards 										AI.XI.A.R3
Collision Avoidance
Clearing Procedures – As able in instrument flight (AIM 4-4-15 Clearing & Scanning Techniques)
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind
Clearly communicate intentions & location in practice areas
Scanning – As able during instrument flight (AIM 4-4-14)
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Movements should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program)
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike (AIM 7-6-4 Obstructions to Flight)
Be familiar with any obstacles near the airport(s) – Charts, Terminal procedures, & NOTAMs
Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL
Supporting guy wire can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 					AI.XI.A.R4
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on performance, especially without visual references
If distracted, recognize the problem, and fix it
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with pre-flight planning - Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Lack of Visual References
Can be very disorienting: Trust the instruments, use automation, ask for help, return to VMC
For more details, see II.B. Visual Scanning & Collision Avoidance and II.M. Night Operations
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
“Attack the closest alligator” – handle the most pressing problem and go from there
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
RM: Control application solely by reference to instruments 			AI.XI.A.R7
The lesson as a whole is basically an RM discussion of control solely by reference to instruments
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

WHAT
Attitude instrument flying may be defined as the control of an aircraft’s spatial position by using instruments rather than outside visual references.

WHY
In the case that you mistakenly fly into adverse weather, or don’t have an outside horizon (night over water, haze, etc.) it is essential to be proficient flying the airplane without outside, visual references.

Establish, then check the altimeter, VSI, and airspeed indicator for desired performance
Crosscheck Errors
RM: Fixation 										AI.XI.A.R5
Staring at a single instrument
Occurs for a variety of reasons and eliminates the crosscheck of other pertinent instruments
RM: Omission 										AI.XI.A.R5
Omitting an instrument from the crosscheck
May be caused by failure to anticipate major instrument indications following attitude changes
Emphasis (VSI chasing is common as is emphasizing pitch or bank instruments)
Putting emphasis on a single instrument, instead of the necessary combination of instruments
We naturally tend to rely on the instrument most understood
RM: Instrument Interpretation 								AI.XI.A.R6
For the crosscheck to be effective, you must understand the information being received
Understand each instrument’s operation and the application of that knowledge to performance
Instrument Operation & Limitations 						AI.XI.A.K1a, AI.XI.A.K1c
Heading Indicator
Gyro turns in a vertical plane, sensing rotation about the plane’s vertical axis
Compass is used to set the appropriate heading, and rigidity causes it to maintain this heading
Precession causes heading to drift & Earth rotates 15o per hour
Precession + rotation means heading should be checked/reset every 15 min
Turn Coordinator
Canted gimbal allowing the gyro to sense both rate of roll as well as rate of turn
A rapid roll rate causes the mini aircraft to bank more steeply than a slow roll rate
Used to establish and maintain a standard-rate turn (3o per second)
Align the wing of the mini aircraft with the turn index
Airspeed Indicator
Differential pressure gauge indicating the difference between pitot and static pressure
Diaphragm receives pressure from pitot tube & instrument case receives pressure from static port
Increasing pitot pressure/decreasing static pressure expands the diaphragm and vice versa
Gearing indicates changes in airspeed
Altimeter
Measures absolute pressure of the ambient air, displays it as feet above selected pressure level
Air pressure tries to compress aneroid wafers while natural springiness tries to expand them
Compression and expansion move gears/linkages to change the altitude displayed
Adjustable barometric scale (Kollsman window)
Errors (Mechanical and Inherent)
Nonstandard Temperature
Warmer than standard air is less dense, pressure levels are farther apart
True altitude > Indicated altitude
Colder than standard air is denser, pressure levels are closer together
True altitude < Indicated altitude
Nonstandard Pressure
High pressure to Low pressure
As pressure decreases, the altimeter registers it as a climb
Pilot descends to maintain altitude
True altitude < Indicated altitude
The opposite applies from Low pressure to High pressure – True alt > Indicated alt
From hot to cold, or from high to low, look out below!
Vertical Speed Indicator
Differential pressure instrument
Diaphragm and casing are connected to static pressure
Diaphragm is directly connected while the case has a delayed connection
During a climb/descent, the diaphragm expands/contracts immediately, while pressure in the case remains the same for a short period
The difference in pressure is displayed as rate of climb
Adjust
Make the necessary adjustments on the attitude indicator, then repeat the process again
The amount of deviation from the desired performance will determine the magnitude of correction
Restrict the attitude indicator’s pitch displacement to 1 bar or ½ bar width up or down
Use a bank angle that approximates the degrees to turn, not to exceed 30o
Smooth, small adjustments lead to smooth, steady control
Straight-and-Level Flight 									AI.XI.A.K1b
Establish: Establish wings level/nose on the horizon on the attitude indicator; adjust power for cruise
Trim: Trim to relieve the control pressures
Crosscheck: Monitor the instruments for any performance deviations from straight-and-level flight
Adjust: Re-establish pitch and/or power to correct for deviations, trim, and repeat
Turns to Headings 										AI.XI.D.K1b
NOTE: Prior to entering the turn, determine turn direction and the angle of bank required
Establish: Use coordinated aileron and rudder to establish the desired bank on the attitude indicator
If a standard rate turn, use the turn coordinator
Adjust pitch to maintain altitude
Trim: Relieve the control pressures
Crosscheck: Monitor the instruments for any performance deviations from the turn
Adjust: Re-establish pitch and/or power to correct for deviations, trim, and repeat
Roll Out
Apply coordinated rudder and aileron pressure to level the wings on the attitude indicator
Depending on the rate of turn, rollout 5-10o before the desired heading
Or use ½ the bank angle or less as a reference for small turns
Adjust pitch and power for straight-and-level flight at cruise, crosscheck, adjust, and repeat
Constant Airspeed Climb 									AI.XI.B.K1b
Establish: Raise the nose to the approximate pitch attitude for the desired climb speed
Approaching climb speed, set power to the climb setting (full)
Trim: Relieve the control pressures
Crosscheck: Monitor the instruments for any performance deviations from the climb
Adjust: Re-establish pitch and/or power to correct for deviations, trim, and repeat
Adjust pitch to maintain the desired climb airspeed (1 bar or ½ bar width movements)
Level Off
Lead the altitude by 10% of the vertical speed (Ex: 500 fpm climb is led by 50’)
Establish - Reduce power, apply elevator pressure toward level flight on the attitude indicator
Trim – Relieve control pressures
Crosscheck - VSI, altimeter and attitude indicator should show level flight – repeat the process

Apply the climb procedures above, and establish the desired bank angle on the attitude indicator
Monitor turn performance on the heading indicator and turn coordinator
Small adjustments to pitch and power may be necessary to maintain airspeed in the turn
The instrument crosscheck will have to be accelerated as there is more information to take in

Approaching descent speed, lower the nose with the attitude indicator to maintain descent speed
Trim: Relieve the control pressures
Crosscheck: Monitor the instruments for any performance deviations from the desired descent
Adjust: Re-establish pitch and/or power to correct for deviations, trim, and repeat
Adjust the pitch attitude to maintain the desired climb airspeed
Level Off
Lead the altitude by 10% of the vertical speed (EX: 500 fpm descent is led by 50’)
Establish - Introduce power and apply smooth steady elevator pressure toward a level attitude
Trim – Relieve control pressures
Crosscheck - VSI, altimeter and attitude indicator should show level flight – repeat the process

Apply the same procedures as above, and establish the desired bank angle on the attitude indicator
Monitor turn performance on the heading indicator and turn coordinator
Small adjustments to pitch and power may be necessary to maintain airspeed in the turn
The instrument crosscheck will have to be accelerated as there is more information to take in

Improper instrument interpretation
Improper control applications
Failure to establish proper pitch, bank, or power adjustments during altitude, heading, speed corrections
Improper entry or level-off procedure (specific to Constant Airspeed Climbs and Descents)
Improper entry or roll-out procedure (specific to Turns to Headings)
Faulty trim procedure

Collision Avoidance

Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind

Scanning – As able during instrument flight (AIM 4-4-14)

Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right

Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late

Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure

Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL

Overhead Wires (may not be lit) span departures & landmarks pilots often follow

Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on performance, especially without visual references
If distracted, recognize the problem, and fix it

Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions

Starts with pre-flight planning - Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Lack of Visual References
Can be very disorienting: Trust the instruments, use automation, ask for help, return to VMC
For more details, see II.B. Visual Scanning & Collision Avoidance and II.M. Night Operations
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
“Attack the closest alligator” – handle the most pressing problem and go from there
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
RM: Control application solely by reference to instruments 			AI.XI.A.R7
The lesson as a whole is basically an RM discussion of control solely by reference to instruments
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

Introduction
How
Overview
Since unusual attitudes (UAs) are not intentional maneuvers, they are often unexpected
Reactions are therefore instinctive and often dangerous, rather than intelligent and deliberate
In a UA, the immediate problem is not how it got there, but what is the aircraft doing and how to get back to straight and level flight as quickly and safely as possible

Environmental Factors
Turbulence or large variations in wind velocity over a short distance

Preflight planning, weather reports, PIREPs, etc. can be used to avoid this weather
Mechanical Factors

May cause departure from normal flight
Ex: Asymmetric flaps, malfunctioning controls, runaway trim, etc.
Instrument Failures
Autopilot Malfunctions 									      AI.XI.E.K4

Disengage the autopilot and fly the airplane
Improper Trim Technique
Failure to keep the plane trimmed can turn a momentary distraction into an unusual attitude
Big Picture: Knowledge of systems and POH procedures helps minimize failures and prevent UAs
Human Factors
VMC to IMC
A loss of the natural horizon significantly increases the chances of spatial disorientation & vertigo
Diversion of Attention
Diverting attention from flying to an anomaly, malfunction, or any other distraction can lead to a UA
Task Saturation
Poor SRM/CRM skills
A major cause of CRM accidents is the failure to maintain an organized flight deck
The margin of safety is the difference between task requirements & pilot capabilities
Fixation
Too much attention is focused on one instrument – keep the crosscheck moving
Sensory Overload/Deprivation
A pilot’s ability to correlate and manage warnings, annunciations, instrument indications is limited
Especially during a UA that can present multiple visual, auditory, and tactile warnings
Confusion can also ensue if expected warnings are not provided when they should be
An effective crosscheck is very important to determine the issue and maintain control
Spatial Disorientation (SD)
Significant factor in many upset accidents
Pilots experience SD or perceive the situation in one of the following ways:
Recognized SD: Pilot recognizes the situation & safely corrects
Unrecognized SD: Unaware of the UA and fails to take corrective action
Incapacitating SD: Unable to recover due to some combination of:
Not understanding the events
Lacking the skills required
Exceeds psychological or physiological ability to cope with the situation
Understanding, training & practice are necessary to maintain situation awareness & recover safely
Flight by Sensory Sensations Other Than Sight
Flight by instinct almost always leads to erroneous corrections
Surprise & Startle Response
Surprise: Unexpected event that violates expectations & affects the mental process used to respond
Startle: Uncontrollable, automatic muscle reflexes, raised heart rate, blood pressure, etc., elicited by exposure to a sudden, intense event that violates a pilot’s expectations
Untrained pilots often experience a state of surprise & startle response to UAs
“We don’t rise to the level of our expectations; we fall to the level of our training”
Failure to practice Basic Attitude Instrument (BAI) flight
If you don’t use it, you lose it – BAI skills diminish if they’re not practiced
See lesson II.A. Human Factors for more details on illusions, spatial disorientation, etc.

Airspeed Indicator: Decreasing airspeed
Altimeter/VSI: Increasing altitude / Positive rate of climb
Turn Coordinator: May indicate a bank
Attitude Indicator: Nose high, a lot of blue
Nose Low Attitudes (Diving Spiral) - Shown by the same instruments but in the opposite directions
Airspeed Indicator: Increasing airspeed
Altimeter/VSI: Decreasing altitude / Negative rate of climb
Turn Coordinator: May indicate a bank
Attitude Indicator: Nose low, a lot of brown

When using analog instruments, recovery is performed without the attitude indicator
If the attitude indicator is spillable its upset limits may have been exceeded and is unreliable
Even if it is operating properly, errors of up to 5o pitch and bank can result
May be inoperative due to mechanical malfunction, and is a reason for the UA
Indications are difficult to interpret in extreme attitudes
Recovery, instead, is performed with the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI, and turn coordinator
Follow the POH recommended recovery procedures if they differ from the information here
With a glass flight deck, the attitude indicator is very helpful and can be used for recovery

Although similar, the recovery procedures for each are different
The basic intent of the nose high recovery is to prevent a stall
The basic intent of the nose low recovery is to prevent over stressing the airplane
Nose High (Climbing Turn) Recovery 							AI.XI.E.K2

Nose High Attitudes – Main Point: Avoid a Stall
If the airspeed is decreasing, or below that desired:
Procedure: The steps listed are made in the sequence below, but occur almost simultaneously
Power – Increase as necessary (in proportion to the deceleration)
Pitch – Apply forward elevator pressure to lower the nose (reduces AOA preventing stall)
Bank – Use coordinated aileron & rudder to level the wings (reference turn coordinator)
After the initial correction, accelerate the cross-check to verify performance
As the altimeter and airspeed needles slow, attitude is approaching level flight
When the needles stop and reverse direction, the aircraft is passing through level flight
Return to the desired altitude, and establish & verify straight-and-level, coordinated cruise flight
Level flight is indicated by reversal and stabilization of the altimeter and airspeed indicator
Straight, coordinated flight is indicated on the turn coordinator by a level aircraft / centered ball
Set power for the desired airspeed once the airspeed is under control
Nose Low (Diving Spiral) Recovery 							AI.XI.E.K2

Nose Low Attitudes – Main Point: Avoid over G-ing 
If the airspeed is increasing, or above that desired:
Procedure
Power – Reduce power to prevent excessive airspeed and loss of altitude
Bank – Use coordinate aileron & rudder to level the wings using the turn coordinator
Leveling the wings prior to raising the nose reduces load factors in the recovery
Pitch – Smoothly raise the nose for level flight
If ground contact is a concern, use whatever back pressure is necessary to survive
All components should be changed simultaneously for a smooth, proficient recovery

Level flight is indicated by reversal & stabilization of the altimeter and airspeed indicator
Straight, coordinated flight is indicated on the turn coordinator by a level aircraft / centered ball

Use the turn coordinator & attitude indicator, if available, to determine and maintain coordinated flight
Skidding and slipping sensations can aggravate disorientation and retard recovery
A nose low recovery could result in excessive G’s and uncoordinated flight
A nose high recovery could result in an uncoordinated stall, and potentially a spin

Failure to recognize an unusual flight attitude
Consequences of attempting to recover from a UA by “feel” rather than by instrument indications

Failure to recognize from instrument indications when the airplane is passing through a level flight attitude

Inadvertent Flight into IMC 									AI.XI.E.K3
Importance of Instrument Flight Skills
Statistics show that a pilot who isn’t trained in instrument flying, or has let their skills erode, loses control after about 10 minutes once forced to rely solely on instruments
Recognize
Anytime a pilot cannot maintain control by reference to the natural horizon, the condition is IMC
Recognize the situation and accept it as a genuine emergency requiring action

The most important concern at this point is to keep the wings level
An uncontrolled turn usually leads to difficulties with control and can lead to disorientation

Don’t over-control – Make smooth and small attitude changes
No more than one bar width movements up or down

Return to the last known VMC (terrain, airspace, etc. permitting)

XI.E. Recovery from Unusual Flight Attitudes
Introduction
How
Overview
Since unusual attitudes (UAs) are not intentional maneuvers, they are often unexpected
Reactions are therefore instinctive and often dangerous, rather than intelligent and deliberate
In a UA, the immediate problem is not how it got there, but what is the aircraft doing and how to get back to straight and level flight as quickly and safely as possible
Unusual Attitude Situations and Conditions 					AI.XI.E.R1, AI.XI.E.R3
Unusual attitudes may result from various situations/conditions, such as:
Preventing Unusual Attitudes (Top Causal Factors: Environmental, Mechanical, Human)       AI.XI.E.K1
Environmental Factors
Turbulence or large variations in wind velocity over a short distance
Clear air turbulence, mountain waves, wind shear, thunderstorms, microbursts
Preflight planning, weather reports, PIREPs, etc. can be used to avoid this weather
Mechanical Factors
Mechanical Failures
May cause departure from normal flight
Ex: Asymmetric flaps, malfunctioning controls, runaway trim, etc.
Instrument Failures
Autopilot Malfunctions 									      AI.XI.E.K4
Can be insidious – the pilot may not be aware there’s a problem until deep in a UA
Disengage the autopilot and fly the airplane
Improper Trim Technique
Failure to keep the plane trimmed can turn a momentary distraction into an unusual attitude
Big Picture: Knowledge of systems and POH procedures helps minimize failures and prevent UAs
Human Factors
VMC to IMC
A loss of the natural horizon significantly increases the chances of spatial disorientation & vertigo
Diversion of Attention
Diverting attention from flying to an anomaly, malfunction, or any other distraction can lead to a UA
Task Saturation
Poor SRM/CRM skills
A major cause of CRM accidents is the failure to maintain an organized flight deck
The margin of safety is the difference between task requirements & pilot capabilities
Fixation
Too much attention is focused on one instrument – keep the crosscheck moving
Sensory Overload/Deprivation
A pilot’s ability to correlate and manage warnings, annunciations, instrument indications is limited
Especially during a UA that can present multiple visual, auditory, and tactile warnings
Confusion can also ensue if expected warnings are not provided when they should be
An effective crosscheck is very important to determine the issue and maintain control
Spatial Disorientation (SD)
Significant factor in many upset accidents
Pilots experience SD or perceive the situation in one of the following ways:
Recognized SD: Pilot recognizes the situation & safely corrects
Unrecognized SD: Unaware of the UA and fails to take corrective action
Incapacitating SD: Unable to recover due to some combination of:
Not understanding the events
Lacking the skills required
Exceeds psychological or physiological ability to cope with the situation
Understanding, training & practice are necessary to maintain situation awareness & recover safely
Flight by Sensory Sensations Other Than Sight
Flight by instinct almost always leads to erroneous corrections
Surprise & Startle Response
Surprise: Unexpected event that violates expectations & affects the mental process used to respond
Startle: Uncontrollable, automatic muscle reflexes, raised heart rate, blood pressure, etc., elicited by exposure to a sudden, intense event that violates a pilot’s expectations
Untrained pilots often experience a state of surprise & startle response to UAs
“We don’t rise to the level of our expectations; we fall to the level of our training”
Failure to practice Basic Attitude Instrument (BAI) flight
If you don’t use it, you lose it – BAI skills diminish if they’re not practiced
See lesson II.A. Human Factors for more details on illusions, spatial disorientation, etc.
RM: Recognizing Unusual Attitudes (Assessment of Unusual Attitudes) 			AI.XI.E.R2
General Rule: If you note an instrument rate of movement or indication other than those associated with basic instrument flight maneuvers, assume a UA and increase the crosscheck to confirm the situation
Two Categories of UAs: Nose high and Nose low attitudes
Nose High Attitudes (Climbing Turn)
Airspeed Indicator: Decreasing airspeed
Altimeter/VSI: Increasing altitude / Positive rate of climb
Turn Coordinator: May indicate a bank
Attitude Indicator: Nose high, a lot of blue
Nose Low Attitudes (Diving Spiral) - Shown by the same instruments but in the opposite directions
Airspeed Indicator: Increasing airspeed
Altimeter/VSI: Decreasing altitude / Negative rate of climb
Turn Coordinator: May indicate a bank
Attitude Indicator: Nose low, a lot of brown
RM: Recovery Basics (Interpreting Flight Instruments) 			AI.XI.E.K2, AI.XI.E.R6
When using analog instruments, recovery is performed without the attitude indicator
If the attitude indicator is spillable its upset limits may have been exceeded and is unreliable
Even if it is operating properly, errors of up to 5o pitch and bank can result
May be inoperative due to mechanical malfunction, and is a reason for the UA
Indications are difficult to interpret in extreme attitudes
Recovery, instead, is performed with the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI, and turn coordinator
Follow the POH recommended recovery procedures if they differ from the information here
With a glass flight deck, the attitude indicator is very helpful and can be used for recovery

Although similar, the recovery procedures for each are different
The basic intent of the nose high recovery is to prevent a stall
The basic intent of the nose low recovery is to prevent over stressing the airplane
Nose High (Climbing Turn) Recovery 							AI.XI.E.K2
Nose High Attitudes – Main Point: Avoid a Stall
If the airspeed is decreasing, or below that desired:
Procedure: The steps listed are made in the sequence below, but occur almost simultaneously
Power – Increase as necessary (in proportion to the deceleration)
Pitch – Apply forward elevator pressure to lower the nose (reduces AOA preventing stall)
Bank – Use coordinated aileron & rudder to level the wings (reference turn coordinator)
After the initial correction, accelerate the cross-check to verify performance
As the altimeter and airspeed needles slow, attitude is approaching level flight
When the needles stop and reverse direction, the aircraft is passing through level flight
Return to the desired altitude, and establish & verify straight-and-level, coordinated cruise flight
Level flight is indicated by reversal and stabilization of the altimeter and airspeed indicator
Straight, coordinated flight is indicated on the turn coordinator by a level aircraft / centered ball
Set power for the desired airspeed once the airspeed is under control
Nose Low (Diving Spiral) Recovery 							AI.XI.E.K2
Nose Low Attitudes – Main Point: Avoid over G-ing 
If the airspeed is increasing, or above that desired:
Procedure
Power – Reduce power to prevent excessive airspeed and loss of altitude
Bank – Use coordinate aileron & rudder to level the wings using the turn coordinator
Leveling the wings prior to raising the nose reduces load factors in the recovery
Pitch – Smoothly raise the nose for level flight
If ground contact is a concern, use whatever back pressure is necessary to survive
All components should be changed simultaneously for a smooth, proficient recovery

As the altimeter and airspeed needles slow, attitude is approaching level flight
When the needles stop and reverse direction, the aircraft is passing through level flight
Return to the desired altitude, and establish & verify straight-and-level, coordinated cruise flight
Level flight is indicated by reversal & stabilization of the altimeter and airspeed indicator
Straight, coordinated flight is indicated on the turn coordinator by a level aircraft / centered ball
Set power for the desired airspeed once the airspeed is under control
Coordination During Recovery
Use the turn coordinator & attitude indicator, if available, to determine and maintain coordinated flight
Skidding and slipping sensations can aggravate disorientation and retard recovery
A nose low recovery could result in excessive G’s and uncoordinated flight
A nose high recovery could result in an uncoordinated stall, and potentially a spin

RM: Hazards
Inadvertent Flight into IMC 									AI.XI.E.K3
Importance of Instrument Flight Skills
Statistics show that a pilot who isn’t trained in instrument flying, or has let their skills erode, loses control after about 10 minutes once forced to rely solely on instruments
Recognize
Anytime a pilot cannot maintain control by reference to the natural horizon, the condition is IMC
Recognize the situation and accept it as a genuine emergency requiring action
RM: Maintain Control (Control Application Solely by Reference to Instruments) 		AI.XI.E.R7
The only way to control the airplane safely is by using and trusting the flight instruments
The most important concern at this point is to keep the wings level
An uncontrolled turn usually leads to difficulties with control and can lead to disorientation
Attitude Control
Trim for hands-off level flight at cruise speed
Don’t over-control – Make smooth and small attitude changes
No more than one bar width movements up or down
Use any aids (autopilot, wing leveler, etc.) 					AI.XI.E.K4
Maintain cruise speed (turns, climbs, descents) until required to slow for landing
For more details, see XI.A-D. Basic Attitude Instrument Flight
Obtain Assistance
ATC, Guard, FSS, etc.
Weather charts - Be aware of expected VMC conditions
Find/Return to VMC
The best option may be to bug your heading, engage the autopilot (if available) & perform a 180o
Return to the last known VMC (terrain, airspace, etc. permitting)
Collision Hazards 										AI.XI.E.R4
Collision Avoidance
Clearing Procedures – As able in instrument flight (AIM 4-4-15 Clearing & Scanning Techniques)
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind
Clearly communicate intentions & location in practice areas
Scanning – As able during instrument flight (AIM 4-4-14)
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Movements should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Operation Lights On (voluntary FAA safety program)
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike (AIM 7-6-4 Obstructions to Flight)
Be familiar with any obstacles near the airport(s) – Charts, Terminal procedures, & NOTAMs
Antenna Towers can reach > 1,000-2,000’ AGL
Supporting guy wire can extend 1,500’ horizontally
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, Task Prioritization 					AI.XI.E.R5
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on performance, especially without visual references
If distracted, recognize the problem, and fix it
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with pre-flight planning - Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Lack of Visual References
Can be very disorienting: Trust the instruments, use automation, ask for help, return to VMC
For more details, see II.B. Visual Scanning & Collision Avoidance and II.M. Night Operations
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
“Attack the closest alligator” – handle the most pressing problem and go from there
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points
